questions.prompt: A is an n×n real matrix with minimal polynomial μ(x). Which are true?
hints: Every polynomial divisible by μ annihilates A.
Factor the relevant power-minus-one polynomials.
questions.solution: If μ=x²+1, A²=−I and A⁴=I, so A is true. For μ=x²+x, diag(0,−1) is a counterexample: its eighth power is diag(0,1), not I. If μ=x²−x+1, (x+1)μ=x³+1, so A³=−I and A⁶=I, proving C. If μ=x²+x+1, (x−1)μ=x³−1, so A³=I, proving D.
questions.theory: The minimal polynomial of a square matrix is the unique monic polynomial of least degree that annihilates it. A polynomial p satisfies p(A)=0 exactly when the minimal polynomial divides p. This allows matrix-power identities to be established through ordinary polynomial factorization without diagonalizing the matrix. If the minimal polynomial has zero constant term, zero is an eigenvalue and the matrix is singular, so no positive power can equal the identity. Quadratic cyclotomic factors often imply finite-order identities. The method is to test divisibility of x^k−1 or use the given quadratic relation recursively. A pitfall is checking eigenvalues alone without accounting for the minimal polynomial, especially when repeated roots permit nontrivial Jordan blocks.

similar_questions.prompt: If μ_A=x²−1, show A²=I.
similar_questions.solution: The defining annihilation relation is μ_A(A)=A²−I=0, so A²=I directly.

similar_questions.prompt: If μ_A=(x−1)², must A²=I?
similar_questions.solution: No. A=[[1,1],[0,1]] has that minimal polynomial but A²=[[1,2],[0,1]]≠I. The repeated-root nilpotent part prevents the proposed identity.

questions.prompt: Two populations have f₁(x)=1 and f₂(x)=6x(1−x), 0<x<1, with equal priors. Under 0–1 loss, which statements about the Bayes classifier are true?

options.D: The probability of misclassifying x to π₂ is 1/√3

hints: With equal priors and equal error costs, select the larger density.
Solve 6x(1−x)>1 and integrate the uniform density on that interval.
questions.solution: Choose π₂ when 6x(1−x)>1, or 6x²−6x+1<0. The roots are a=(3−√3)/6 and b=(3+√3)/6, so the decision region is (a,b), proving A and disproving B,C. For a true π₁ observation, the probability of erroneous assignment to π₂ is ∫_a^b1 dx=b−a=1/√3, proving D under the standard class-conditional misclassification convention. If one instead includes the prior probability of π₁, the joint error event has probability 1/(2√3). Ties at the endpoints can be assigned arbitrarily and have probability zero.
questions.theory: A Bayes classifier under zero–one loss selects the class with the greatest posterior probability. Equal prior probabilities reduce this to comparing class densities. The resulting error probabilities are usually reported conditionally on the true class: P(classify as j|true class i). Multiplying such an error by the prior gives its contribution to the overall Bayes error. These are distinct quantities and should be labeled. A quadratic density comparison may produce a central interval rather than a one-sided threshold. The method is to solve the likelihood inequality, specify the two decision regions and integrate the true-class density over the erroneous region. Points where densities tie have zero probability for continuous laws and do not affect the risk.

similar_questions.solution: 2x>1 means x>1/2. Under class 1, the error is ∫_(1/2)^1dx=1/2.

similar_questions.prompt: In that example find class-2 error and overall error.
similar_questions.solution: Class-2 error is ∫₀^(1/2)2x dx=1/4. Overall equal-prior error is (1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/4)=3/8.

In a one-dimensional closed segment the endpoints are the vertices, while interior points remain feasible but are not vertices. A linear objective on a compact segment attains its minimum and maximum at endpoints unless it is constant. The method is to simplify the constraints before enumerating candidates. A common pitfall is applying full-dimensional vertex tests without noticing equality constraints implied by inequalities.

options.D: There are infinitely many closed subsets of cardinality 5

questions.solution: The atoms are {0} and {−n,n}, n≥1. Every union of atoms is open, and its complement is another such union, so those and only those sets are closed. ℕ∪{0} is not a union of atoms and is not closed. It meets every nonempty atom and hence every nonempty open set, so it is dense. A finite closed set excluding zero consists of two-element atoms and has even size. Choosing zero and any two distinct pairs gives a closed five-element set, with infinitely many choices. Thus B,C,D.
questions.theory: A partition topology consists of all unions of blocks of a partition. If the proposed generators are disjoint and cover the space, finite intersections create no additional nonempty sets, so the generated topology is exactly this partition topology. Every block union is clopen because its complement is another block union. A subset is dense precisely when it meets every block; otherwise a missed block is a nonempty open set disjoint from it. Closed-set cardinalities are determined by sizes of the included blocks. The method is to identify the atomic partition, translate closedness and density into block conditions and then count possibilities. A pitfall is assuming individual integers are separable when positive and negative partners share every neighborhood.

questions.solution: The quotient ℤ[√−7]/(√−7) is ℤ/7ℤ, a field, so (√−7) is prime and A holds. Divisibility by 4 would require 3+√−7=4(a+b√−7), giving 4a=3,4b=1, impossible. The element 4 divides 2×2 but does not divide 2, so it is not prime. If a+b√−7 is a unit, its positive integer norm a²+7b² must equal 1. This forces b=0,a=±1, and both are units. Hence D holds.
questions.theory: In an integral domain, a nonzero nonunit p is prime when p divides a product only by dividing a factor. Equivalently its principal ideal is prime, so the quotient by that ideal is an integral domain. For a quadratic integer ring ℤ[√−d], the conjugation norm N(a+b√−d)=a²+db² is multiplicative and takes nonnegative integer values. A unit must have norm one, because the norms of it and its inverse multiply to one. Divisibility can also be tested by equating the independent rational-basis coefficients. The method combines the quotient criterion for primeness and norms for units. Do not assume every irreducible is prime in a general quadratic ring, and do not confuse this ring with the larger full ring of integers of its field.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the units of ℤ[i].
similar_questions.solution: N(a+bi)=a²+b²=1 gives (a,b)=(±1,0),(0,±1). Thus units are ±1,±i.

similar_questions.prompt: Is 3 prime in ℤ[i]?
similar_questions.solution: The quotient is 𝔽₃[t]/(t²+1). The polynomial has no root in 𝔽₃ and is irreducible, so the quotient is a field. Therefore 3 is prime.

These normal equations arise from orthogonality of the residual to each predictor and to constants; joint normality is not required. The explained variance is Cov(Y,Z)S⁻¹Cov(Z,Y), and the multiple correlation coefficient is its square root after dividing by Var Y. Correlation is nonnegative in this convention. The method is to partition the supplied covariance correctly and retain means in the intercept. A pitfall is using marginal simple-regression slopes without adjusting for correlation among predictors.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true?

options.A: Every uncountable set has nonzero Lebesgue measure
options.C: Numbers in [0,1] whose decimal expansion does not contain 7 have measure zero
options.D: For ℚ={a₁,a₂,…} and S=⋃ₖ≥1(aₖ−1/k³,aₖ+1/k³), S\T has positive measure for every closed T⊆ℝ

hints: Use Cantor-type interval coverings for the digit-restricted sets.
A universal statement about every closed T must include T=ℝ.
questions.solution: A is false: the usual Cantor set is uncountable and has measure zero. After m base-five digits, G lies in 2^m intervals each of length 5^(−m), giving outer measure ≤(2/5)^m→0, so B is false. Avoiding one decimal digit gives at most 9^m intervals of length 10^(−m), total (9/10)^m→0; ambiguous decimal endpoints form a countable set and do not change the conclusion. Thus C holds. For D choose T=ℝ, which is closed and makes S\T empty.
questions.theory: Lebesgue measure is not determined by cardinality: countable sets have measure zero, but uncountable sets can also be null. Digit-restricted sets provide constructive examples. Fixing the first m digits locates numbers in intervals whose lengths equal the base to the negative mth power. If only k digits are allowed in base b with k<b, at most k^m such intervals suffice, giving total length (k/b)^m, which tends to zero. This is an outer-measure argument and proves measurability for null sets. Nonunique terminating expansions affect only countably many endpoints. The method is to build arbitrarily small interval covers and to test universal quantifiers with extreme allowed choices. Do not mistake a first-stage retained proportion for the final measure.

similar_questions.prompt: Find measure of numbers in [0,1] with ternary digits only 0 and 2.
similar_questions.solution: At stage m they lie in 2^m intervals of length 3^(−m). The total cover length is (2/3)^m→0, so the Cantor set has measure zero.

similar_questions.prompt: Find measure of numbers with decimal digits from {0,1,2,3,4}.
similar_questions.solution: There are at most 5^m first-m-digit cylinders, each length 10^(−m). Their total length is (1/2)^m→0, so the set is null.

The polynomial x⁸−2 is Eisenstein at 2, so [ℚ(β):ℚ]=8, proving C. Since β⁴=√2, the intermediate field ℚ(√2) has degree 2 and [ℚ(β):ℚ(√2)]=8/2=4. questions.theory: The degree of a finite field extension is its dimension as a vector space over the base field. For a tower K⊆F⊆L, the tower law gives [L:K]=[L:F][F:K]. This creates divisibility restrictions on possible subfields. A cubic over ℚ is irreducible if it has no rational root, while Eisenstein’s criterion proves irreducibility when one prime divides every nonleading coefficient, does not divide the leading coefficient and its square does not divide the constant term. A known root’s extension degree then gives the degree of its minimal polynomial over an intermediate field. The method here combines an absolute irreducibility result with the tower law. Avoid applying Eisenstein naively with irrational coefficients when a rational polynomial already gives the needed information.

options.B: For f∈BV, there are monotonic f₁,f₂ with limₓ→a⁺f(x)=infₓ∈(a,b)f₁(x)−infₓ∈(a,b)f₂(x)

Monotone functions have at most countably many discontinuities and are Riemann integrable on a compact interval.
questions.solution: Jordan decomposition writes f=f₁−f₂ with f₁,f₂ increasing and bounded. Thus f is measurable, proving A. The right limit of each increasing function at a equals its infimum on (a,b), so B holds. Their finite left limits at b also exist, proving C. Each bounded monotone function is Riemann integrable, and the difference of two such functions is Riemann integrable. Therefore every BV function is Riemann integrable, and only D is false.
questions.theory: A function has bounded variation on [a,b] when the supremum of sums Σ|f(x_i)−f(x_(i−1))| over finite partitions is finite. Jordan’s decomposition theorem says exactly that such a function is the difference of two bounded increasing functions. Increasing functions have finite one-sided limits at interior and endpoint positions, are measurable and have at most countably many discontinuities. They are Riemann integrable on compact intervals, either by a direct upper/lower-sum argument or Lebesgue’s criterion. These properties pass to a difference, except monotonicity itself. Endpoint values may differ from one-sided limits without affecting integrability. The method is to use the decomposition once and transfer each requested property. Do not confuse bounded variation with continuity: jumps are allowed.

similar_questions.prompt: Is the step function 1_{[1/2,1]} of bounded variation and Riemann integrable?

similar_questions.prompt: Does f(x)=sin x have bounded variation on [0,π]?
similar_questions.solution: It rises from zero to one and falls to zero, so total variation is two. It is continuous and thus Riemann integrable, with integral two.

Conversely if h is invariant, take g=h and its average is h. Hence D.
questions.theory: Invariance under a finite cyclic rotation can be analyzed through Taylor coefficients. If ζ is a primitive mth root of unity, f(ζz)=f(z) implies a_n(ζ^n−1)=0, so only powers divisible by m occur. This permits many nonconstant functions, unlike invariance under a strict contraction. Averaging over a finite group is a projection onto its invariant functions: applying the average twice gives the same result, and reindexing proves symmetry. For disk-valued functions, convexity of the target ensures their finite mean remains disk-valued. The method is to test monomials and then construct the group average. A pitfall is assuming a periodic rotational identity forces constancy or bounds polynomial degree by the rotation order.

similar_questions.prompt: For m=2, describe the invariant holomorphic functions.
similar_questions.solution: The identity is f(−z)=f(z), so only even Taylor powers occur. Examples include z² and any disk-valued even holomorphic function.

similar_questions.prompt: Average g(z)=z+z³ over cube-root rotations.
similar_questions.solution: The z term averages to zero because 1+ζ+ζ²=0. The z³ term is unchanged under every rotation. The average is z³.

questions.prompt: yᵢ=β₀+icβ₁+εᵢ, i=1,…,n,n>2, with uncorrelated errors of mean zero and variance one. For the BLUEs, Cov(β̂₀,β̂₁)=1. Which are true?

questions.solution: With c≠0, Gauss–Markov gives Cov(β̂₀,β̂₁)=−x̄/S_xx=−6/[cn(n−1)]. Equating to one yields c=−6/[n(n−1)]=6/[n(1−n)], proving C and disproving D. Intercept variance is 1/n+x̄²/S_xx=1/n+3(n+1)/[n(n−1)]=2(2n+1)/[n(n−1)], proving A and excluding B. The positive specified covariance is consistent with negative c, because the predictor mean then is negative.
questions.theory: For simple linear regression with uncorrelated equal-variance errors and full-rank design, ordinary least squares is the best linear unbiased estimator by the Gauss–Markov theorem. Its slope variance is σ²/S_xx, intercept variance σ²(1/n+x̄²/S_xx) and intercept-slope covariance −σ²x̄/S_xx. Equally spaced predictors x_i=ci yield explicit sums from Σi and Σi², with S_xx=c²n(n²−1)/12. The sign of the covariance is opposite the predictor mean, while intercept variance is unchanged by a nonzero scaling of all predictors. The method is to substitute the spacing into the standard covariance formulas and solve for c. A pitfall is overlooking negative spacing or allowing c=0, which destroys slope estimability.

similar_questions.prompt: For predictors −1,0,1 and error variance one, find intercept-slope covariance.

similar_questions.prompt: For n=3 and c=−1, find the covariance.
similar_questions.solution: x̄=−2 and S_xx=2, so covariance=−(−2)/2=1, matching the formula −6/[c×3×2].

questions.prompt: For α∈ℕ, f(x,y)=xyᵅ/(x²+y²) away from zero and f(0,0)=0. Which are true?

options.A: f is continuous on ℝ² for every α≥1
options.B: f is differentiable on ℝ² for every α≥3

hints: Use homogeneity or a radius bound at zero.
Compute fₓ(0,y) before taking its derivative in y at zero.
questions.solution: For α=1, along x=y≠0, f=1/2, so A is false. Both axis restrictions are zero, giving the partials in C. With r=√(x²+y²), |f|≤r^(α−1); for α≥3, |f|/r≤r^(α−2)→0, proving differentiability at zero with derivative zero. Elsewhere it is smooth, so B holds. For y≠0, fₓ(0,y)=y^(α−2). Its y derivative at zero is one when α=3, and zero when α>3. Thus the “every α≥3” claim D is false. B,C only.
questions.theory: For rational functions singular only at the origin, continuity and differentiability are decided by controlling the numerator relative to the radial distance. A homogeneous function of degree k satisfies a scaling law, and if bounded on the unit circle its size is O(r^k). Differentiability with zero derivative follows when that degree exceeds one. Axis restrictions may give zero partial derivatives even when continuity fails, so partials cannot replace a full radial test. Mixed partial derivatives must be computed in the printed order, using the first partial as a function along the second coordinate axis. The method separates the exponent threshold for continuity, first differentiability and mixed derivatives. A pitfall is overlooking a boundary exponent where a power becomes exactly linear and its derivative is nonzero.

similar_questions.prompt: For f=xy²/(x²+y²), is f continuous at zero?
similar_questions.solution: It has degree one and |f|≤r, so it tends to zero. However along x=y=t its value is t/2, preventing a zero linear derivative despite zero axis partials.

similar_questions.prompt: For α=4 in the stated family, compute ∂ᵧ∂ₓf(0,0).
similar_questions.solution: fₓ(0,y)=y² for nonzero y and is zero at zero. Its derivative at zero is lim y²/y=0.

questions.prompt: Which functions are uniformly continuous on their stated intervals?
hints: A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz bound for the first two functions.
Extend the third continuously to its finite closed interval; use the distance-function inequality for the fourth.
questions.solution: For A, write N=cos²x,D=1+x²+sin²x. Since |N′|≤1,D≥1+x² and |D′|≤2x+1, |f′|≤1+(2x+1)/(1+x²)², uniformly bounded. For B, f′=−sin(1/x)/x²−cos(1/x)/x³, bounded by two on x≥1. Thus both are Lipschitz. For C, |xsin(2/(πx))|≤x gives limit zero at zero; its other endpoint limit exists, so it extends continuously to [0,π/2] and is uniformly continuous. The distance to a nonempty set satisfies |d(x,A)−d(y,A)|≤|x−y|, so D is 1-Lipschitz. All four hold.
questions.theory: Uniform continuity requires one closeness threshold that works simultaneously for every pair of domain points. A bounded derivative on an interval gives a global Lipschitz bound by the mean value theorem, hence uniform continuity even on an unbounded interval. On a bounded open interval, a continuous extension to the compact closure gives uniform continuity by Heine–Cantor. Rapidly oscillating factors do not prevent such an extension when their amplitude tends to zero. Distance to a nonempty set is always 1-Lipschitz by the triangle inequality, independently of whether the set is closed. The method selects a suitable sufficient criterion for each function rather than one criterion for all. A pitfall is assuming every continuous function on an unbounded or open interval is uniformly continuous.

similar_questions.prompt: Is xsin(1/x), extended by zero, uniformly continuous on [0,1]?
similar_questions.solution: It is continuous at zero because its modulus is at most x, and continuous elsewhere. Compactness then gives uniform continuity.

similar_questions.prompt: Is distance to {0} uniformly continuous on ℝ?
similar_questions.solution: The function is |x| and satisfies ||x|−|y||≤|x−y|, so it is 1-Lipschitz and uniformly continuous.

questions.prompt: On C[0,1], d(f,g)=∫₀¹|f−g|. For n≥2, fₙ=0 on [0,1/2], fₙ=n(t−1/2) on [1/2,1/2+1/n], and fₙ=1 afterward. Which are true?

options.A: fₙ is Cauchy in this metric
options.B: This metric space is not complete
options.C: The pointwise limit exists at every t
options.D: The pointwise limit, if it exists, belongs to C[0,1]

hints: The pointwise limit is a step function with a jump at one-half.
Compute the L¹ area between each ramp and the step.
questions.solution: The pointwise limit is F(t)=0 for t≤1/2 and F(t)=1 for t>1/2, so C holds and D fails. The distance in L¹ to F is the small triangular area 1/(2n). Thus d(fₙ,f_m)≤1/(2n)+1/(2m)→0, proving A. If a continuous g were a metric limit, it would agree with F almost everywhere by uniqueness of L¹ limits. Continuity would then force g=0 throughout (0,1/2) and g=1 throughout (1/2,1), impossible at the junction. Thus the Cauchy sequence has no limit in C[0,1], proving incompleteness B.
questions.theory: Completeness is a property of a space together with its chosen metric. Continuous functions are complete under the supremum norm, but not under the integral absolute-difference metric. In the latter, narrow transition regions can become negligible, allowing continuous ramps to approach a discontinuous step in L¹. A Cauchy sequence need not converge within a noncomplete space. Pointwise convergence is a separate notion and does not itself determine metric convergence, though here direct area estimates connect them. Uniqueness of L¹ limits is up to equality almost everywhere, and no continuous representative can realize a genuine step jump. The method is to construct a Cauchy sequence and exclude every possible continuous metric limit. A pitfall is importing completeness from the usual sup-norm function space.

similar_questions.prompt: Are continuous functions complete under the uniform metric?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. A uniformly Cauchy sequence converges uniformly to a real-valued limit, and uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the L¹ distance from a width-ε linear ramp rising from zero to one to the instantaneous step at its left endpoint.
similar_questions.solution: The difference region is a triangle with base ε and height one, so the integral absolute difference is ε/2.

questions.prompt: If xₙ₊₁=xₙ+αf(xₙ), α∈ℝ, converges to the root of f(x)=e^(−x)−sin x in [0,π/2] for every x₀ in that interval, which statements are true?

The printed implication asks for a necessary interval, rather than whether each interval is sufficient.
questions.solution: Let gα(x)=x+α(e^(−x)−sin x). For every 0<α<1, g′=1−α(e^(−x)+cos x), whose absolute value on I=[0,π/2] is at most max{|1−2α|,|1−αe^(−π/2)|}<1. Also g maps I into itself: for x beyond the unique root, g≤x and g≥x−sin x≥0; before the root g≥x, and convexity g″=α(e^(−x)+sin x)>0 bounds the maximum by endpoint values, both in I. Hence Banach’s theorem gives convergence for every initial point and every α∈(0,1). In particular α=0.85 satisfies the premise but none of A–D. Therefore none is a valid necessary conclusion as printed. Conditional intended wording “which ranges ensure convergence?” would make all four ranges sufficient, hence A,B,C,D. The source’s reversed implication prevents a literal unambiguous key.
questions.theory: A fixed-point iteration converges from every point of a closed interval if its map sends that interval into itself and is a strict contraction there. A uniform derivative bound below one supplies the contraction condition by the mean value theorem. For root iteration x↦x+αf(x), the sign and magnitude of α control derivative bounds; f′<0 favors positive relaxation. A sufficient range of parameters is logically different from a necessary range inferred from observed convergence. Listing several disjoint sufficient subintervals does not permit inferring which one contains an unspecified convergent parameter. The method checks invariance, contraction and the exact direction of the statement. A pitfall is silently replacing “if converges, then α lies here” by “if α lies here, then converges.”

similar_questions.prompt: For xₙ₊₁=(1−α)xₙ on ℝ, find the convergence range to zero.
similar_questions.solution: For every initial value, convergence requires |1−α|<1, namely 0<α<2. Individual smaller subintervals are sufficient but are not necessary.

similar_questions.prompt: If α∈(0.2,0.4) guarantees convergence, does convergence imply α∈(0.2,0.4)?
similar_questions.solution: No. The implication may hold for a larger parameter range. A convergent example at α=0.8 disproves the converse without contradicting the stated sufficiency.

questions.prompt: A bead of unit mass slides on the smooth wire y=x² under gravity g. With horizontal coordinate x(t), which are true?

Use L=T−V and the Euler–Lagrange equation in generalized coordinate x.
questions.solution: Unit mass gives T=(1/2)(ẋ²+ẏ²)=(1/2)(1+4x²)ẋ². With zero potential at y=0, V=gy=gx². Hence L=(1/2)(1+4x²)ẋ²−gx², disproving A and proving B,C. Now ∂L/∂ẋ=(1+4x²)ẋ, so its time derivative is (1+4x²)ẍ+8xẋ². Also ∂L/∂x=4xẋ²−2gx. Subtraction yields (1+4x²)ẍ+4xẋ²+2gx=0, proving D.
questions.theory: A smooth frictionless wire imposes a holonomic constraint, allowing one generalized coordinate to describe the bead’s motion. The kinetic energy must include every Cartesian velocity component after substituting the constraint; for a graph y=h(x), T=(m/2)(1+h′(x)²)ẋ². Gravitational potential is mgh(x) up to an additive constant. The Lagrangian L=T−V gives the equation through d/dt(∂L/∂ẋ)−∂L/∂x=0. Differentiating a coordinate-dependent kinetic factor introduces an additional velocity-squared term. The method is to eliminate the constraint before differentiation and carefully use the product rule. A pitfall is treating ẋ alone as the bead’s full speed or inserting an incorrect mass or potential factor. Energy is conserved because this Lagrangian has no explicit time dependence and the constraint is fixed.

similar_questions.prompt: For a unit bead on y=2x, find T and V.
similar_questions.solution: ẏ=2ẋ, so T=(1/2)(1+4)ẋ²=(5/2)ẋ². Potential is V=2gx, giving equation 5ẍ+2g=0.

similar_questions.prompt: For y=x³, write the unit-mass kinetic energy.
similar_questions.solution: ẏ=3x²ẋ. Therefore T=(1/2)(1+9x⁴)ẋ² and V=gx³.

questions.prompt: In a two-component system, each component’s failures follow a Poisson process of intensity λ>0. Which are true?
hints: Each marginal first-failure time is exponential, but this does not specify their dependence.
Compare independent component processes with components sharing exactly the same Poisson process.
questions.solution: The printed hypotheses do not say the two component failure processes are independent. They may be the same Poisson process, so both fail together; then series and parallel reliability are both e^(−λt), and both hazards equal λ. Thus none of A–D is guaranteed by the literal source. Conditional intended independent-component derivation: put q=e^(−λt). Series reliability q² and hazard 2λ make A,B true; parallel reliability 1−(1−q)²=2q−q² makes C true. Its hazard is −R′/R=2λ(1−q)/(2−q), not the expression in D. Under that additional hypothesis the intended set is A,B,C. Missing independence is a genuine source issue, so no unconditional key is assigned.
questions.theory: Reliability R(t)=P(T>t) describes survival until time t, and hazard r(t)=−R′(t)/R(t) gives the instantaneous failure rate conditional on survival. A Poisson failure process of rate λ has exponential first-event time and marginal reliability e^(−λt). A series system survives when both components survive, while a parallel system survives when at least one does. Product formulas for these joint events require independence; marginal Poisson assumptions alone do not determine their probabilities. Perfectly dependent component processes provide a direct counterexample. Even with independence, a parallel system does not have a constant hazard, and the survival denominator must be retained. The method is to establish the joint dependence model before multiplying reliabilities and differentiating.

similar_questions.prompt: Two independent exponential components have rates a,b. Find series reliability and hazard.
similar_questions.solution: Series survival is e^(−at)e^(−bt)=e^(−(a+b)t), so its hazard is a+b.

similar_questions.prompt: Two identical-rate independent components are in parallel. Find hazard at t=0 and its limit as t→∞.
similar_questions.solution: Hazard is 2λ(1−q)/(2−q), q=e^(−λt). At zero q=1, giving zero; as t→∞ q→0, the hazard tends to λ.
